questions.question: How do you detect and diagnose a Java memory leak in production?
questions.title: Java Memory Leak Detection — Heap Dump Analysis
questions.direct_answer: Memory leaks in Java occur when references prevent GC from collecting objects. Symptoms: gradual heap growth, full GC frequency increasing, eventual OOM. Diagnose with heap dumps (jmap or -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError) analyzed in Eclipse MAT or JProfiler.

sections.title: The GC Works Correctly — Leaked Objects Stay Alive Because Something Still References Them
sections.content:
Memory leaks in Java are not about the garbage collector failing — the GC works exactly as designed. A leak occurs when objects that are no longer logically needed remain reachable through a chain of strong references from a **GC root** (static fields, thread stacks, JNI references). Because the GC only collects unreachable objects, these accidentally retained objects accumulate indefinitely.

The symptoms follow a predictable pattern. **Heap usage after full GC** climbs gradually over hours or days. Full GC frequency increases as the available heap shrinks. Eventually the JVM throws `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` or, if the GC is spending most of its time collecting with diminishing returns, `OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded`.

The most frequent leak sources in production Spring Boot applications are **static collections** that grow without eviction (unbounded caches, listener registries that never unsubscribe), **ThreadLocal values** not cleaned up on thread pool threads where threads are recycled across requests, and **classloader leaks** during hot redeployment in application servers where a single retained reference pins an entire classloader and all its loaded classes in memory. The common but wrong fix is increasing `-Xmx` — this delays the crash by hours but never resolves the root cause.

Diagnosis requires capturing a **heap dump** at the right moment and tracing the reference chain from the suspected objects back to their GC root.

sections.title: From Symptom to Root Cause: The Heap Dump Diagnostic Workflow
sections.content:
The first step is confirming that the problem is actually a leak rather than insufficient heap sizing. Run `jstat -gc <pid> 5000` to sample heap occupancy every five seconds and observe the heap usage after each full GC cycle. If the **post-full-GC baseline** is stable, the heap is simply undersized — increase `-Xmx`. If it trends upward over hours, a leak is confirmed.

Capture a heap dump using one of two approaches. The proactive approach adds `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps/` to JVM startup flags — when OOM finally hits, the JVM writes a snapshot automatically. The on-demand approach uses `jmap -dump:format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>`, but be aware this pauses the JVM briefly on large heaps.

Open the dump in **Eclipse MAT** and run the automated Leak Suspects report. MAT identifies which object types are accumulating disproportionately and shows example reference chains. The **Dominator Tree** view ranks objects by retained heap size — the object at the top of the tree is often the collection or cache that is hoarding memory. Follow the reference chain from the suspect back to its GC root to understand why the GC cannot collect it.

Common fixes include replacing unbounded `HashMap` caches with size-limited alternatives like **Caffeine** with `maximumSize` and `expireAfterWrite`, adding `ThreadLocal.remove()` calls in `finally` blocks for request-scoped values, and implementing proper `unsubscribe` methods for event listener registries.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Memory leaks = objects reachable from GC roots but no longer needed** — GC is correct; something holds the reference.
- **Confirm with `jstat -gc`** — watch post-full-GC heap baseline; creeping upward over hours = leak; stable = undersized heap.
- **Root cause: heap dump + Eclipse MAT** — Leak Suspects report + Dominator Tree show which objects retain the most memory.
- **Common sources: static collections, ThreadLocal without remove(), listener registries that never unsubscribe**.
- **Always deploy with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`** — you won't be able to reproduce OOM after a restart.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Memory leaks in Java happen when objects that are no longer needed remain reachable through a chain of strong references to a GC root — the GC is doing its job correctly, but something is holding the reference.

**Confirming the leak:**
- Run `jstat -gc <pid>` and watch the post-full-GC heap baseline
- Baseline creeping upward over hours → leak; stays flat but GC runs constantly → heap undersized

**Root cause analysis:**
- Capture heap dump: on-demand with `jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>` or via `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`
- Open in Eclipse MAT: run Leak Suspects report; Dominator Tree shows which objects retain the most memory
- Follow the reference chain from the suspect to its GC root — reveals exactly why the object can't be collected

**Most common sources:**
- Static collections that grow without bounds
- `ThreadLocal` values not removed on thread-pool threads — `try-finally remove()` is mandatory
- Listener/observer registries that subscribe but never unsubscribe

I recommend deploying with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` enabled and using Caffeine or Guava Cache — unbounded `HashMap` caches are the single most common leak pattern in production.

questions.question: What is the difference between StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError in Java?
questions.title: StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError in Java
questions.direct_answer: StackOverflowError occurs when the thread's call stack exceeds its fixed size, typically due to infinite or very deep recursion. OutOfMemoryError occurs when the JVM cannot allocate memory — either the heap is full (Java heap space), metaspace is full, or too many threads have been created. Both are Errors (not Exceptions), meaning they indicate serious JVM-level problems that generally should not be caught.

sections.title: Two Errors That Map to Two Completely Different Memory Regions
sections.content:
Both `StackOverflowError` and `OutOfMemoryError` extend `java.lang.Error`, signaling conditions the application generally cannot recover from. But they originate in completely different parts of the JVM memory model and require entirely different diagnostic approaches.

**StackOverflowError** means a single thread's call stack — a fixed-size, per-thread memory area that stores method frames — has run out of space. The default stack size ranges from 512KB to 1MB depending on the platform, configurable with `-Xss`. Each method call pushes a frame containing local variables, operand stack, and return address. When the stack is full, typically after thousands of recursive calls without a base case, the JVM throws this error on that specific thread.

**OutOfMemoryError** means the JVM cannot allocate memory from a shared resource — and it comes in several distinct flavors. "Java heap space" means the garbage collector cannot free enough heap for a new allocation. "Metaspace" means too many classes have been loaded, common during hot redeployment in application servers. "GC overhead limit exceeded" means the JVM is spending 98% of its time in garbage collection while recovering less than 2% of the heap — the JVM gives up rather than thrashing indefinitely.

The key diagnostic difference: **StackOverflowError** is diagnosed from the **thread stack trace** (the recursive method is visible), while OOM is diagnosed from a **heap dump** showing what objects are consuming memory.

sections.title: OOM Subtypes, Causes, and the Diagnostic Tool for Each
sections.content:
Knowing which OOM subtype you are dealing with determines the entire diagnostic approach. Each subtype maps to a different memory region and a different root cause.

| Error | Memory Region | Common Cause | Diagnostic Tool |
|---|---|---|---|
| StackOverflowError | Thread stack | Infinite or deep recursion | Thread dump — recursive method visible in stack |
| OOM: Java heap space | Heap | Memory leak or undersized heap | Heap dump with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` |
| OOM: Metaspace | Native (Metaspace) | Classloader leak, excessive codegen | `jcmd VM.classloader_stats`, cap with `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` |
| OOM: GC overhead limit | Heap | Near-full heap thrashing GC | Same as heap space — analyze retained objects |
| OOM: unable to create native thread | OS native memory | Unbounded thread creation | `jstack` thread count, switch to thread pools |

**StackOverflowError** almost always has an obvious fix. The stack trace itself shows the recursive method, and the fix is adding a proper base case or converting the recursion to an iterative approach with an explicit stack data structure. Increasing `-Xss` is rarely correct — it treats the symptom by allowing deeper recursion instead of fixing the unbounded recursion itself, and it increases the memory footprint of every thread in the application.

**OOM: Java heap space** requires more investigation. Set `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` before the problem occurs so the JVM captures a snapshot at the moment of failure. Open the dump in Eclipse MAT, check the Dominator Tree for the largest retained objects, and follow reference chains to understand why the GC cannot reclaim them. The root cause is usually a collection that grows without bounds, a cache without eviction, or a genuine need for more heap — distinguished by whether the post-full-GC live set is stable or growing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **StackOverflowError = thread stack exhausted** — almost always deep/infinite recursion; fix the base case, not -Xss.
- **OOM "Java heap space"** — GC can't free enough memory; leak if post-GC live set grows, undersized if stable.
- **OOM "Metaspace"** — classloader leak; common during hot redeployment in application servers.
- **OOM "GC overhead limit exceeded"** — JVM spends 98% of time collecting less than 2%; effectively a leak.
- **OOM "unable to create native thread"** — unbounded thread creation exhausted OS thread limits.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`StackOverflowError` and `OutOfMemoryError` are Java's two most common JVM-level fatal errors — they affect completely different memory regions, have different root causes, and require entirely different diagnosis approaches.

**StackOverflowError:**
- A single thread's call stack runs out of space — almost always from infinite or very deep recursion
- Stack trace shows the recursive method directly — straightforward to diagnose
- Fix: add a base case or convert to iteration; increasing `-Xss` rarely helps

**OutOfMemoryError subtypes:**
- "Java heap space": GC can't free enough memory — either a leak (post-GC live set grows over time) or undersized heap (post-GC live set stable)
- "Metaspace": classloader leak — common during hot redeployment in app servers
- "GC overhead limit exceeded": JVM spends 98% of time collecting less than 2% — effectively a leak under pressure
- "unable to create native thread": unbounded thread creation exhausted OS thread limits

**Both extend Error:**
- Signals the JVM is in a state you generally cannot safely recover from — don't `catch` and continue

I recommend setting `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` in every production deployment — the snapshot is essential for root cause analysis and you don't want to scramble to reproduce after a container restart.
